claims.statement: For a qualifying Polish commercial transaction, statutory late-payment interest arises without a reminder only when the creditor performed its obligation and payment was not received by the contractual due date; an overdue invoice alone does not prove those conditions.

Polish law gives the creditor a fixed EUR 40, EUR 70, or EUR 100 recovery-cost entitlement by claim size and permits additional recovery costs only in a justified amount; the fixed compensation claim itself cannot be assigned.

For 1 July through 31 December 2026, the official Polish annual late-payment rates are 11.75% where the debtor is a public healthcare entity and 13.75% otherwise, confirming that calculations must be effective-date versioned.

The EU Payment Observatory reports that 52% of European companies faced late-payment problems in 2024, Poland was among the worst-affected Member States, and companies averaged 9.85 hours per week chasing late payments; this establishes a material loss class, not purchase or delegation willingness.

The European Commission says businesses, especially SMEs, remain reluctant to claim interest and compensation because they fear damaging commercial relationships, directly weakening the assumption that statutory entitlement converts routinely into an outsourced paid event.

The creditor remains the source of authority: Polish Civil Code Articles 95-101 provide that representation operates only within authority granted by the represented party, general authority must be written, and a power of attorney is generally revocable at any time.

If the servicing relationship is legally characterized as a mandate or an unregulated services contract, Civil Code Articles 746 and 750 allow the client to terminate at any time and prohibit advance waiver of termination for important reasons; a 12-month term therefore does not itself create irrevocable control or a for-cause-only mandate.

A written portfolio servicing agreement and authority instrument appear legally constructible, but the evidence does not establish that exclusivity can make the operational control durable against revocation or termination; specialist Polish contract advice and executed customer terms are required.

Civil-court representation is limited to enumerated representatives, with mandatory advocate or legal-counsel representation in specified proceedings; the founder company cannot assume that a commercial servicing mandate alone authorizes every litigation or enforcement step.

Processing debtor and contact-person data requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimization, accuracy, security, and role-appropriate contracting; Article 28 requires a binding processor contract when the service acts for a controller.

The proposed cross-client data advantage cannot be assumed from access to servicing data: reuse for model training or benchmarking would require compatible purposes, suitable controller-processor roles, instructions, and contractual rights beyond merely collecting a claim.

Kaczmarski's WinGO is a close operating substitute: a business can upload one unpaid invoice online, pay only after successful recovery, track the case in software, and receive amicable collection with a recommendation for court escalation; its reported 80% recovery figure is vendor-reported and not independently verified.

InsERT already embeds Kaczmarski collection into accounting programs with a few-click invoice handoff, customer approval over decisions, and published post-recovery commissions of 5-14% for claims up to 365 days late, rising to 18% beyond 730 days; this proves the channel exists for an incumbent, not that it is available to the founder.

Kaczmarski's general price list quotes 17% of recovered value with a PLN 640 minimum for amicable collection and prices court-enforcement work individually, creating a visible price benchmark but no evidence for the candidate's recovery rate, service cost, or margin.

Statistics Poland surveyed 89 debt-collection enterprises for 2024; they accepted 917,000 corporate claims with PLN 13.865 billion nominal value and held 1.895 million active corporate claims worth PLN 52.511 billion at year end, demonstrating substantial incumbent capacity and competition rather than an open control point.

The candidate's illustrative PLN 500 million annual administered-principal target equals about 3.6% of all corporate claim face value accepted during 2024 by the 89 collectors in the GUS survey; definitions are not perfectly comparable, but the ratio makes the required distribution scale plainly nontrivial.
No executed contract, signed pilot, or buyer interview establishes that Polish SMEs will grant this new entrant a 12-month exclusive mandate over a defined receivables portfolio.

No private commercial evidence establishes willingness to pay the proposed split of 2-8% of principal plus 10-20% of statutory amounts, or willingness to renew the mandate annually after accounting for debtor-relationship effects.

Fully loaded contribution economics remain unknown because segment-specific recovery probability, time to cash, dispute and evidence-exception labor, partner and court costs, refunds, bad-debt outcomes, channel share, CAC, support, insurance, and compliance overhead have not been measured together.

No retained Polish counsel opinion or executed collection-law-firm agreement establishes the exact boundary between automatable administration, debtor-facing legal activity, civil representation, and enforcement, nor the partner price, acceptance criteria, SLA, or liability allocation.

No customer contract, controller assessment, or data-processing schedule grants reusable cross-client rights in invoice, contact, dispute, or resolution data sufficient to build the claimed data moat.
No accountant or bookkeeper has committed to refer portfolios, integrate data, accept exclusivity, or disclosed a viable referral share and customer-acquisition cost for this entrant.
The share of target-sector overdue invoices that are undisputed, supported by complete performance and delivery evidence, solvent, and collectible without intensive legal work is unknown.

There is no operating evidence that onboarding, debtor disputes, reconciliations, client approvals, complaints, partner handoffs, and reporting can remain within the founder's five-hour daily limit at meaningful portfolio scale.

No tested contract or payment flow establishes authority to receive recovered money, reconcile partial payments, deduct a contingency fee, and remit the balance without creating avoidable custody, accounting, tax, or client-money risk.

Because incumbents already offer the core workflow, embedded accounting-software distribution, relationship-sensitive amicable collection, success fees, tracking, and legal escalation, any defensible advantage would have to come from verified recovery uplift, lower fully loaded cost, or contracted proprietary access; none is presently evidenced.
